books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Lecompton Constitution, Article VII, Section 1 (1857). Public domain. Wording verified against the excerpts at the Harry S. Truman Library (trumanlibrary.gov, Lecompton Constitution lesson).
stimulus.text: The right of property is before and higher than any constitutional sanction, and the right of the owner of a slave to such slave and its increase is the same and as inviolable as the right of the owner of any property whatever.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Lecompton Constitution described slavery as

options.text: a moral evil to be ended.
options.misconception: The passage calls slavery a property right “before and higher than any constitutional sanction,” not an evil.

options.text: a property right no constitution could touch.

options.misconception: The passage protects slavery forever, not for a time; it bars emancipation without the owner’s consent.

options.text: a choice for voters to make.
options.misconception: The passage does not leave slavery to the voters; it declares the right inviolable.

rationales.A: The passage calls slavery a property right “before and higher than any constitutional sanction,” not an evil.
rationales.B: “The right of property is before and higher than any constitutional sanction,” and the owner’s right is “inviolable.”
rationales.C: The passage protects slavery forever, not for a time; it bars emancipation without the owner’s consent.
rationales.D: The passage does not leave slavery to the voters; it declares the right inviolable.
rationales.general:
1. Read the claim: the right of property stands before and higher than any constitution.
2. Read the reach: the owner’s right to a slave is as inviolable as to any property whatever.
3. See the lock: no legislature could emancipate slaves without paying the owners in full.
Remember: when a constitution calls a right higher than itself, it is locking the door against future voters.
